# ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this workflow for ARC-style grid tasks, including lifelong streams where each instance is independent and demonstrations, wrong submissions, and attempts may carry different costs.

## 1. Respect the interaction contract

- Identify the exact required response format before solving. If the environment requires exactly one JSON action on the final line, provide exactly that action and no competing output format.
- Track demo requests, wrong attempts, and attempt caps. A request for another demonstration is an information-gathering action, not a free pause; use it only when its expected information is worth its cost.
- Keep the current instance separate from prior tasks unless the task explicitly says instances recur with the same rule. Repeated task IDs can indicate a learned rule, but do not assume access to prior conversations.
- If the task has a defined terminal action, use it only when the environment says the instance is over or permits ending it.

## 2. Parse the grid before hypothesizing

- Record dimensions, background color, non-background colors, and all repeated shapes.
- Segment objects by 4-neighbor connectivity first. If shapes touch only diagonally, note that 8-neighbor grouping would produce a different interpretation; choose the grouping supported by the examples.
- For repeated blocks, record each object's bounding box and top-left coordinate. Distinguish object origins from individual colored cells, and do not treat overlapping 2x2 windows as separate objects.
- Make a compact inventory: object shape, color, location, size, adjacency, alignments, and any repeated spacing or symmetry.
- For each demonstration, compare input and output cell-by-cell conceptually: determine what changed, what stayed fixed, and whether dimensions or background changed. Treat unchanged examples as constraints too.

## 3. Infer a compact, reusable rule

- Prefer a simple rule that explains every demonstration, not a list of coordinates or a rule fitted only to the latest input.
- Test likely ARC operations: recolor by shape/size/count, select outliers, complete symmetry, connect or group nearby objects, copy/reflect/rotate, sort or move by position, and use one object as a marker or template.
- Check whether selection is at the object, component, row/column, or whole-pattern level. If adjacent identical blocks form a larger connected object, compare both the elementary-block and merged-component interpretations.
- Explicitly test a candidate against every positive and negative example. Ask: what distinguishes selected objects from visually similar unselected ones? If no stable discriminator is supported, keep uncertainty explicit rather than inventing a confident rule.
- When multiple hypotheses survive, identify what new demonstration would discriminate between them. Request it only if the information gain is likely to prevent a costlier wrong submission.

## 4. Construct and verify the output

- Start from an exact copy of the test grid and apply only the inferred changes.
- Preserve dimensions, row lengths, and every unaffected cell. For recoloring, change all and only the cells belonging to selected objects.
- Before submitting, verify that the output follows the same rule used for all demonstrations, that no object was omitted or accidentally merged, and that the serialized grid contains only integers in the allowed range.
- If feedback says incorrect and the task remains active, use that information to update the hypothesis; do not repeat the same output unchanged.

## 5. Manage reasoning and tool use

- Delegate only genuinely independent analyses, and provide each analyst with the same precise object inventory and exact question. Avoid repeated redundant delegation; compare distinct hypotheses rather than accumulating near-identical guesses.
- Prefer a concise object table or coordinate list over repeatedly transcribing whole grids. Mark coordinates clearly as zero- or one-indexed and specify whether they identify top-left cells or component bounds.
- Do not encode an unverified pattern as a rule. A single demonstration may permit many explanations; more data or a safer explicit uncertainty estimate is preferable to false certainty.

## Pitfalls

- Miscounting objects when 2x2 motifs touch or overlap; verify bounding boxes and connectivity.
- Mixing coordinate conventions or describing a component as a singleton when its adjacent blocks make a larger component.
- Inferring selection by location from one sample when the rule may depend on shape, grouping, symmetry, or a relation among objects.
- Spending demo requests without articulating which uncertainty the next example is meant to resolve.
- Submitting prose or extra formatting when the benchmark requires only a machine-readable action.

description: Use when solving ARC grid transformation puzzles.

# ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this workflow for ARC-style grid tasks, including lifelong streams where each instance is independent and demonstrations, wrong submissions, and attempts may carry different costs.

## 1. Respect the interaction contract

- Identify the exact required response format before solving. If the environment requires exactly one JSON action on the final line, provide exactly that action and no competing output format.
- Track demo requests, wrong attempts, and attempt caps. A request for another demonstration is an information-gathering action, not a free pause; use it only when its expected information is worth its cost.
- Keep the current instance separate from prior tasks unless the task explicitly says instances recur with the same rule. Repeated task IDs can indicate a learned rule, but do not assume access to prior conversations.
- If the task has a defined terminal action, use it only when the environment says the instance is over or permits ending it.

## 2. Parse the grid before hypothesizing

- Record dimensions, background color, non-background colors, and all repeated shapes.
- Segment objects by 4-neighbor connectivity first. If shapes touch only diagonally, note that 8-neighbor grouping would produce a different interpretation; choose the grouping supported by the examples.
- For repeated blocks, record each object's bounding box and top-left coordinate. Distinguish object origins from individual colored cells, and do not treat overlapping 2x2 windows as separate objects.
- Make a compact inventory: object shape, color, location, size, adjacency, alignments, and any repeated spacing or symmetry.
- For each demonstration, compare input and output cell-by-cell conceptually: determine what changed, what stayed fixed, and whether dimensions or background changed. Treat unchanged examples as constraints too.

## 3. Infer a compact, reusable rule

- Prefer a simple rule that explains every demonstration, not a list of coordinates or a rule fitted only to the latest input.
- Test likely ARC operations: recolor by shape/size/count, select outliers, complete symmetry, connect or group nearby objects, copy/reflect/rotate, sort or move by position, and use one object as a marker or template.
- Check whether selection is at the object, component, row/column, or whole-pattern level. If adjacent identical blocks form a larger connected object, compare both the elementary-block and merged-component interpretations.
- Explicitly test a candidate against every positive and negative example. Ask: what distinguishes selected objects from visually similar unselected ones? If no stable discriminator is supported, keep uncertainty explicit rather than inventing a confident rule.
- When multiple hypotheses survive, identify what new demonstration would discriminate between them. Request it only if the information gain is likely to prevent a costlier wrong submission.

## 4. Construct and verify the output

- Start from an exact copy of the test grid and apply only the inferred changes.
- Preserve dimensions, row lengths, and every unaffected cell. For recoloring, change all and only the cells belonging to selected objects.
- Before submitting, verify that the output follows the same rule used for all demonstrations, that no object was omitted or accidentally merged, and that the serialized grid contains only integers in the allowed range.
- If feedback says incorrect and the task remains active, use that information to update the hypothesis; do not repeat the same output unchanged.

## 5. Manage reasoning and tool use

- Delegate only genuinely independent analyses, and provide each analyst with the same precise object inventory and exact question. Avoid repeated redundant delegation; compare distinct hypotheses rather than accumulating near-identical guesses.
- Prefer a concise object table or coordinate list over repeatedly transcribing whole grids. Mark coordinates clearly as zero- or one-indexed and specify whether they identify top-left cells or component bounds.
- Do not encode an unverified pattern as a rule. A single demonstration may permit many explanations; more data or a safer explicit uncertainty estimate is preferable to false certainty.

## Pitfalls

- Miscounting objects when 2x2 motifs touch or overlap; verify bounding boxes and connectivity.
- Mixing coordinate conventions or describing a component as a singleton when its adjacent blocks make a larger component.
- Inferring selection by location from one sample when the rule may depend on shape, grouping, symmetry, or a relation among objects.
- Spending demo requests without articulating which uncertainty the next example is meant to resolve.
- Submitting prose or extra formatting when the benchmark requires only a machine-readable action.

# ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this workflow for ARC-style grid tasks, including lifelong streams where each instance is independent and demonstrations, wrong submissions, and attempts may carry different costs.

## 1. Respect the interaction contract

- Identify the exact required response format before solving. If the environment requires exactly one JSON action on the final line, provide exactly that action and no competing output format.
- Track demo requests, wrong attempts, and attempt caps. A request for another demonstration is an information-gathering action, not a free pause; use it only when its expected information is worth its cost.
- Keep the current instance separate from prior tasks unless the task explicitly says instances recur with the same rule. Repeated task IDs can indicate a learned rule, but do not assume access to prior conversations.
- If the task has a defined terminal action, use it only when the environment says the instance is over or permits ending it.

## 2. Parse the grid before hypothesizing

- Record dimensions, background color, non-background colors, and all repeated shapes.
- Segment objects by 4-neighbor connectivity first. If shapes touch only diagonally, note that 8-neighbor grouping would produce a different interpretation; choose the grouping supported by the examples.
- For repeated blocks, record each object's bounding box and top-left coordinate. Distinguish object origins from individual colored cells, and do not treat overlapping 2x2 windows as separate objects.
- Make a compact inventory: object shape, color, location, size, adjacency, alignments, and any repeated spacing or symmetry.
- For each demonstration, compare input and output cell-by-cell conceptually: determine what changed, what stayed fixed, and whether dimensions or background changed. Treat unchanged examples as constraints too.

## 3. Infer a compact, reusable rule

- Prefer a simple rule that explains every demonstration, not a list of coordinates or a rule fitted only to the latest input.
- Test likely ARC operations: recolor by shape/size/count, select outliers, complete symmetry, connect or group nearby objects, copy/reflect/rotate, sort or move by position, and use one object as a marker or template.
- Check whether selection is at the object, component, row/column, or whole-pattern level. If adjacent identical blocks form a larger connected object, compare both the elementary-block and merged-component interpretations.
- Explicitly test a candidate against every positive and negative example. Ask: what distinguishes selected objects from visually similar unselected ones? If no stable discriminator is supported, keep uncertainty explicit rather than inventing a confident rule.
- When multiple hypotheses survive, identify what new demonstration would discriminate between them. Request it only if the information gain is likely to prevent a costlier wrong submission.

## 4. Construct and verify the output

- Start from an exact copy of the test grid and apply only the inferred changes.
- Preserve dimensions, row lengths, and every unaffected cell. For recoloring, change all and only the cells belonging to selected objects.
- Before submitting, verify that the output follows the same rule used for all demonstrations, that no object was omitted or accidentally merged, and that the serialized grid contains only integers in the allowed range.
- If feedback says incorrect and the task remains active, use that information to update the hypothesis; do not repeat the same output unchanged.

## 5. Manage reasoning and tool use

- Delegate only genuinely independent analyses, and provide each analyst with the same precise object inventory and exact question. Avoid repeated redundant delegation; compare distinct hypotheses rather than accumulating near-identical guesses.
- Prefer a concise object table or coordinate list over repeatedly transcribing whole grids. Mark coordinates clearly as zero- or one-indexed and specify whether they identify top-left cells or component bounds.
- Do not encode an unverified pattern as a rule. A single demonstration may permit many explanations; more data or a safer explicit uncertainty estimate is preferable to false certainty.

## Pitfalls

- Miscounting objects when 2x2 motifs touch or overlap; verify bounding boxes and connectivity.
- Mixing coordinate conventions or describing a component as a singleton when its adjacent blocks make a larger component.
- Inferring selection by location from one sample when the rule may depend on shape, grouping, symmetry, or a relation among objects.
- Spending demo requests without articulating which uncertainty the next example is meant to resolve.
- Submitting prose or extra formatting when the benchmark requires only a machine-readable action.

D=[([(0,0),(0,11),(1,4),(2,7),(5,15)],[(3,1),(3,13),(4,10),(5,6)]), ([(0,12),(4,3),(4,7)],[(1,1),(1,4),(2,9)]), ([(1,13),(3,8),(4,5),(5,0)],[(0,6),(2,2),(5,11)])]
for j,(S,N) in enumerate(D,1):
 p=np.array([(r,c) for r,c in S],float); A=np.c_[2*p[:,0],2*p[:,1],np.ones(len(p))]; b=(p*p).sum(1); x=np.linalg.lstsq(A,b,rcond=None)[0]; center=x[:2]; rad=np.sqrt(max(0,x[2]+center@center)); residual=np.linalg.norm(p-center,axis=1)-rad
 print(j,'circle center',center,'R',rad,'resid',np.round(residual,2))
 # Fit line PCA max errors
 u,s,v=np.linalg.svd(p-p.mean(0),full_matrices=False); perp=(p-p.mean(0))@v[1]; print('line residual',np.round(perp,2))

**Analyzing convex hulls**

I’m looking into the D2 positives triangle, which includes points like (0,12), (4,3), and (4,7). The negatives—(1,1), (1,4), and (2,9)—might be mostly outside, but (2,9) seems to be inside the triangle. This suggests that the criterion selected is the vertices of the convex hull. For D3, I'm considering positives like (1,13) and (5,0), while some negatives could lie outside. It's a complex evaluation of hulls and their boundaries!

**Exploring demo patterns**

I'm thinking about analyzing each demo, focusing on how positives and negatives might relate to a **vanishing point**. It seems that patterns could lie at **intersections of diagonal guides**. I wonder if all selected points are on the same side of a **linear boundary**, but the positive points seem scattered. # ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this workflow for ARC-style grid tasks, including lifelong streams where each instance is independent and demonstrations, wrong submissions, and attempts may carry different costs.

## 1. Respect the interaction contract

- Identify the exact required response format before solving. If the environment requires exactly one JSON action on the final line, provide exactly that action and no competing output format.
- Track demo requests, wrong attempts, and attempt caps. A request for another demonstration is an information-gathering action, not a free pause; use it only when its expected information is worth its cost.
- Keep the current instance separate from prior tasks unless the task explicitly says instances recur with the same rule. Repeated task IDs can indicate a learned rule, but do not assume access to prior conversations.
- If the task has a defined terminal action, use it only when the environment says the instance is over or permits ending it.

## 2. Parse the grid before hypothesizing

- Record dimensions, background color, non-background colors, and all repeated shapes.
- Segment objects by 4-neighbor connectivity first. If shapes touch only diagonally, note that 8-neighbor grouping would produce a different interpretation; choose the grouping supported by the examples.
- For repeated blocks, record each object's bounding box and top-left coordinate. Distinguish object origins from individual colored cells, and do not treat overlapping 2x2 windows as separate objects.
- Make a compact inventory: object shape, color, location, size, adjacency, alignments, and any repeated spacing or symmetry.
- For each demonstration, compare input and output cell-by-cell conceptually: determine what changed, what stayed fixed, and whether dimensions or background changed. Treat unchanged examples as constraints too.

## 3. Infer a compact, reusable rule

- Prefer a simple rule that explains every demonstration, not a list of coordinates or a rule fitted only to the latest input.
- Test likely ARC operations: recolor by shape/size/count, select outliers, complete symmetry, connect or group nearby objects, copy/reflect/rotate, sort or move by position, and use one object as a marker or template.
- Check whether selection is at the object, component, row/column, or whole-pattern level. If adjacent identical blocks form a larger connected object, compare both the elementary-block and merged-component interpretations.
- Explicitly test a candidate against every positive and negative example. Ask: what distinguishes selected objects from visually similar unselected ones? If no stable discriminator is supported, keep uncertainty explicit rather than inventing a confident rule.
- When multiple hypotheses survive, identify what new demonstration would discriminate between them. Request it only if the information gain is likely to prevent a costlier wrong submission.

## 4. Construct and verify the output

- Start from an exact copy of the test grid and apply only the inferred changes.
- Preserve dimensions, row lengths, and every unaffected cell. For recoloring, change all and only the cells belonging to selected objects.
- Before submitting, verify that the output follows the same rule used for all demonstrations, that no object was omitted or accidentally merged, and that the serialized grid contains only integers in the allowed range.
- If feedback says incorrect and the task remains active, use that information to update the hypothesis; do not repeat the same output unchanged.

## 5. Manage reasoning and tool use

- Delegate only genuinely independent analyses, and provide each analyst with the same precise object inventory and exact question. Avoid repeated redundant delegation; compare distinct hypotheses rather than accumulating near-identical guesses.
- Prefer a concise object table or coordinate list over repeatedly transcribing whole grids. Mark coordinates clearly as zero- or one-indexed and specify whether they identify top-left cells or component bounds.
- Do not encode an unverified pattern as a rule. A single demonstration may permit many explanations; more data or a safer explicit uncertainty estimate is preferable to false certainty.

## Pitfalls

- Miscounting objects when 2x2 motifs touch or overlap; verify bounding boxes and connectivity.
- Mixing coordinate conventions or describing a component as a singleton when its adjacent blocks make a larger component.
- Inferring selection by location from one sample when the rule may depend on shape, grouping, symmetry, or a relation among objects.
- Spending demo requests without articulating which uncertainty the next example is meant to resolve.
- Submitting prose or extra formatting when the benchmark requires only a machine-readable action.

from itertools import combinations
from fractions import Fraction
D=[([(0,0),(0,11),(1,4),(2,7),(5,15)],[(3,1),(3,13),(4,10),(5,6)]), ([(0,12),(4,3),(4,7)],[(1,1),(1,4),(2,9)]), ([(1,13),(3,8),(4,5),(5,0)],[(0,6),(2,2),(5,11)])]
def circle3(P):
 (r1,c1),(r2,c2),(r3,c3)=P
 # x=c y=r, solve 2x*cx +2y*cy + k = x2+y2
 rows=[(2*c,2*r,c*c+r*r) for r,c in P]
 (a,b,d),(e,f,g),(h,i,j)=rows
 det=a*(f*1-i*1)-b*(e-h)+(e*i-f*h) # easier use determinant 3x3?
 # solve 2x2 differences: (a-e)cx+(b-f)cy=d-g; (a-h)cx+(b-i)cy=d-j
 A,B,C=d-g,d-j
 u,v,w=a-e,b-f,a-h
 y,z,x=e # dummy
 den=u*(b-i)-v*(a-h)
 if den==0:return None
 cx=Fraction(A*(b-i)-v*C,den); cy=Fraction(u*C-A*(a-h),den)
 return cx,cy
for k,(T,N) in enumerate(D):
 print('demo',k+1)
 for triple in combinations(T,3):
  circ=circle3(triple)
  if not circ:continue
  cx,cy=circ
  rr=(cx**2+cy**2)-0 # radius square relative origin; x=c, y=r
  vals=[(Fraction(c)-cx)**2+(Fraction(r)-cy)**2 for r,c in T]
  inT=[p for p,v in zip(T,vals) if v==vals[0]]
  inN=[p for p in N if (Fraction(p[1])-cx)**2+(Fraction(p[0])-cy)**2==vals[0]]
  if len(inT)>=3:
   print(' circle',triple,'center',cx,cy,'targets_on',inT,'neg_on',inN)

from itertools import combinations
from fractions import Fraction
D=[([(0,0),(0,11),(1,4),(2,7),(5,15)],[(3,1),(3,13),(4,10),(5,6)]), ([(0,12),(4,3),(4,7)],[(1,1),(1,4),(2,9)]), ([(1,13),(3,8),(4,5),(5,0)],[(0,6),(2,2),(5,11)])]
def circle3(P):
 rows=[(2*c,2*r,c*c+r*r) for r,c in P]
 (a,b,d),(e,f,g),(h,i,j)=rows
 A,C=d-g,d-j; u,v=a-e,b-f; w,z=a-h,b-i
 den=u*z-v*w
 if den==0:return None
 return (Fraction(A*z-v*C,den),Fraction(u*C-A*w,den))
for k,(T,N) in enumerate(D):
 print('demo',k+1)
 found=[]
 for triple in combinations(T,3):
  circ=circle3(triple)
  if not circ:continue
  cx,cy=circ
  rr=(Fraction(triple[0][1])-cx)**2+(Fraction(triple[0][0])-cy)**2
  onT=[p for p in T if (Fraction(p[1])-cx)**2+(Fraction(p[0])-cy)**2==rr]
  onN=[p for p in N if (Fraction(p[1])-cx)**2+(Fraction(p[0])-cy)**2==rr]
  if len(onT)>=3: found.append((triple,cx,cy,onT,onN))
 print(found)

# ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this workflow for ARC-style grid tasks, including lifelong streams where each instance is independent and demonstrations, wrong submissions, and attempts may carry different costs.

## 1. Respect the interaction contract

- Identify the exact required response format before solving. If the environment requires exactly one JSON action on the final line, provide exactly that action and no competing output format.
- Track demo requests, wrong attempts, and attempt caps. A request for another demonstration is an information-gathering action, not a free pause; use it only when its expected information is worth its cost.
- Keep the current instance separate from prior tasks unless the task explicitly says instances recur with the same rule. Repeated task IDs can indicate a learned rule, but do not assume access to prior conversations.
- If the task has a defined terminal action, use it only when the environment says the instance is over or permits ending it.

## 2. Parse the grid before hypothesizing

- Record dimensions, background color, non-background colors, and all repeated shapes.
- Segment objects by 4-neighbor connectivity first. If shapes touch only diagonally, note that 8-neighbor grouping would produce a different interpretation; choose the grouping supported by the examples.
- For repeated blocks, record each object's bounding box and top-left coordinate. Distinguish object origins from individual colored cells, and do not treat overlapping 2x2 windows as separate objects.
- Make a compact inventory: object shape, color, location, size, adjacency, alignments, and any repeated spacing or symmetry.
- For each demonstration, compare input and output cell-by-cell conceptually: determine what changed, what stayed fixed, and whether dimensions or background changed. Treat unchanged examples as constraints too.

## 3. Infer a compact, reusable rule

- Prefer a simple rule that explains every demonstration, not a list of coordinates or a rule fitted only to the latest input.
- Test likely ARC operations: recolor by shape/size/count, select outliers, complete symmetry, connect or group nearby objects, copy/reflect/rotate, sort or move by position, and use one object as a marker or template.
- Check whether selection is at the object, component, row/column, or whole-pattern level. If adjacent identical blocks form a larger connected object, compare both the elementary-block and merged-component interpretations.
- Explicitly test a candidate against every positive and negative example. Ask: what distinguishes selected objects from visually similar unselected ones? If no stable discriminator is supported, keep uncertainty explicit rather than inventing a confident rule.
- When multiple hypotheses survive, identify what new demonstration would discriminate between them. Request it only if the information gain is likely to prevent a costlier wrong submission.

## 4. Construct and verify the output

- Start from an exact copy of the test grid and apply only the inferred changes.
- Preserve dimensions, row lengths, and every unaffected cell. For recoloring, change all and only the cells belonging to selected objects.
- Before submitting, verify that the output follows the same rule used for all demonstrations, that no object was omitted or accidentally merged, and that the serialized grid contains only integers in the allowed range.
- If feedback says incorrect and the task remains active, use that information to update the hypothesis; do not repeat the same output unchanged.

## 5. Manage reasoning and tool use

- Delegate only genuinely independent analyses, and provide each analyst with the same precise object inventory and exact question. Avoid repeated redundant delegation; compare distinct hypotheses rather than accumulating near-identical guesses.
- Prefer a concise object table or coordinate list over repeatedly transcribing whole grids. Mark coordinates clearly as zero- or one-indexed and specify whether they identify top-left cells or component bounds.
- Do not encode an unverified pattern as a rule. A single demonstration may permit many explanations; more data or a safer explicit uncertainty estimate is preferable to false certainty.

## Pitfalls

- Miscounting objects when 2x2 motifs touch or overlap; verify bounding boxes and connectivity.
- Mixing coordinate conventions or describing a component as a singleton when its adjacent blocks make a larger component.
- Inferring selection by location from one sample when the rule may depend on shape, grouping, symmetry, or a relation among objects.
- Spending demo requests without articulating which uncertainty the next example is meant to resolve.
- Submitting prose or extra formatting when the benchmark requires only a machine-readable action.

# ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this workflow for ARC-style grid tasks, including lifelong streams where each instance is independent and demonstrations, wrong submissions, and attempts may carry different costs.

## 1. Respect the interaction contract

- Identify the exact required response format before solving. If the environment requires exactly one JSON action on the final line, provide exactly that action and no competing output format.
- Track demo requests, wrong attempts, and attempt caps. A request for another demonstration is an information-gathering action, not a free pause; use it only when its expected information is worth its cost.
- Keep the current instance separate from prior tasks unless the task explicitly says instances recur with the same rule. Repeated task IDs can indicate a learned rule, but do not assume access to prior conversations.
- If the task has a defined terminal action, use it only when the environment says the instance is over or permits ending it.

## 2. Parse the grid before hypothesizing

- Record dimensions, background color, non-background colors, and all repeated shapes.
- Segment objects by 4-neighbor connectivity first. If shapes touch only diagonally, note that 8-neighbor grouping would produce a different interpretation; choose the grouping supported by the examples.
- For repeated blocks, record each object's bounding box and top-left coordinate. Distinguish object origins from individual colored cells, and do not treat overlapping 2x2 windows as separate objects.
- Make a compact inventory: object shape, color, location, size, adjacency, alignments, and any repeated spacing or symmetry.
- For each demonstration, compare input and output cell-by-cell conceptually: determine what changed, what stayed fixed, and whether dimensions or background changed. Treat unchanged examples as constraints too.

## 3. Infer a compact, reusable rule

- Prefer a simple rule that explains every demonstration, not a list of coordinates or a rule fitted only to the latest input.
- Test likely ARC operations: recolor by shape/size/count, select outliers, complete symmetry, connect or group nearby objects, copy/reflect/rotate, sort or move by position, and use one object as a marker or template.
- Check whether selection is at the object, component, row/column, or whole-pattern level. If adjacent identical blocks form a larger connected object, compare both the elementary-block and merged-component interpretations.
- Explicitly test a candidate against every positive and negative example. Ask: what distinguishes selected objects from visually similar unselected ones? If no stable discriminator is supported, keep uncertainty explicit rather than inventing a confident rule.
- When multiple hypotheses survive, identify what new demonstration would discriminate between them. Request it only if the information gain is likely to prevent a costlier wrong submission.

## 4. Construct and verify the output

- Start from an exact copy of the test grid and apply only the inferred changes.
- Preserve dimensions, row lengths, and every unaffected cell. For recoloring, change all and only the cells belonging to selected objects.
- Before submitting, verify that the output follows the same rule used for all demonstrations, that no object was omitted or accidentally merged, and that the serialized grid contains only integers in the allowed range.
- If feedback says incorrect and the task remains active, use that information to update the hypothesis; do not repeat the same output unchanged.

## 5. Manage reasoning and tool use

- Delegate only genuinely independent analyses, and provide each analyst with the same precise object inventory and exact question. Avoid repeated redundant delegation; compare distinct hypotheses rather than accumulating near-identical guesses.
- Prefer a concise object table or coordinate list over repeatedly transcribing whole grids. Mark coordinates clearly as zero- or one-indexed and specify whether they identify top-left cells or component bounds.
- Do not encode an unverified pattern as a rule. A single demonstration may permit many explanations; more data or a safer explicit uncertainty estimate is preferable to false certainty.

## Pitfalls

- Miscounting objects when 2x2 motifs touch or overlap; verify bounding boxes and connectivity.
- Mixing coordinate conventions or describing a component as a singleton when its adjacent blocks make a larger component.
- Inferring selection by location from one sample when the rule may depend on shape, grouping, symmetry, or a relation among objects.
- Spending demo requests without articulating which uncertainty the next example is meant to resolve.
- Submitting prose or extra formatting when the benchmark requires only a machine-readable action.

name: arc-puzzle-solving
description: Use when solving ARC grid transformation puzzles.
---

# ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this workflow for ARC-style grid tasks, including lifelong streams where each instance is independent and demonstrations, wrong submissions, and attempts may carry different costs.

## 1. Respect the interaction contract

- Identify the exact required response format before solving. If the environment requires exactly one JSON action on the final line, provide exactly that action and no competing output format.
- Track demo requests, wrong attempts, and attempt caps. A request for another demonstration is an information-gathering action, not a free pause; use it only when its expected information is worth its cost.
- Keep the current instance separate from prior tasks unless the task explicitly says instances recur with the same rule. Repeated task IDs can indicate a learned rule, but do not assume access to prior conversations.
- If the task has a defined terminal action, use it only when the environment says the instance is over or permits ending it.

## 2. Parse the grid before hypothesizing

- Record dimensions, background color, non-background colors, and all repeated shapes.
- Segment objects by 4-neighbor connectivity first. If shapes touch only diagonally, note that 8-neighbor grouping would produce a different interpretation; choose the grouping supported by the examples.
- For repeated blocks, record each object's bounding box and top-left coordinate. Distinguish object origins from individual colored cells, and do not treat overlapping 2x2 windows as separate objects.
- Make a compact inventory: object shape, color, location, size, adjacency, alignments, and any repeated spacing or symmetry.
- For each demonstration, compare input and output cell-by-cell conceptually: determine what changed, what stayed fixed, and whether dimensions or background changed. Treat unchanged examples as constraints too.

## 3. Infer a compact, reusable rule

- Prefer a simple rule that explains every demonstration, not a list of coordinates or a rule fitted only to the latest input.
- Test likely ARC operations: recolor by shape/size/count, select outliers, complete symmetry, connect or group nearby objects, copy/reflect/rotate, sort or move by position, and use one object as a marker or template.
- Check whether selection is at the object, component, row/column, or whole-pattern level. If adjacent identical blocks form a larger connected object, compare both the elementary-block and merged-component interpretations.
- Explicitly test a candidate against every positive and negative example. Ask: what distinguishes selected objects from visually similar unselected ones? If no stable discriminator is supported, keep uncertainty explicit rather than inventing a confident rule.
- When multiple hypotheses survive, identify what new demonstration would discriminate between them. Request it only if the information gain is likely to prevent a costlier wrong submission.

## 4. Construct and verify the output

- Start from an exact copy of the test grid and apply only the inferred changes.
- Preserve dimensions, row lengths, and every unaffected cell. For recoloring, change all and only the cells belonging to selected objects.
- Before submitting, verify that the output follows the same rule used for all demonstrations, that no object was omitted or accidentally merged, and that the serialized grid contains only integers in the allowed range.
- If feedback says incorrect and the task remains active, use that information to update the hypothesis; do not repeat the same output unchanged.

## 5. Manage reasoning and tool use

- Delegate only genuinely independent analyses, and provide each analyst with the same precise object inventory and exact question. Avoid repeated redundant delegation; compare distinct hypotheses rather than accumulating near-identical guesses.
- Prefer a concise object table or coordinate list over repeatedly transcribing whole grids. Mark coordinates clearly as zero- or one-indexed and specify whether they identify top-left cells or component bounds.
- Do not encode an unverified pattern as a rule. A single demonstration may permit many explanations; more data or a safer explicit uncertainty estimate is preferable to false certainty.

## Pitfalls

- Miscounting objects when 2x2 motifs touch or overlap; verify bounding boxes and connectivity.
- Mixing coordinate conventions or describing a component as a singleton when its adjacent blocks make a larger component.
- Inferring selection by location from one sample when the rule may depend on shape, grouping, symmetry, or a relation among objects.
- Spending demo requests without articulating which uncertainty the next example is meant to resolve.
- Submitting prose or extra formatting when the benchmark requires only a machine-readable action.

# ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this workflow for ARC-style grid tasks, including lifelong streams where each instance is independent and demonstrations, wrong submissions, and attempts may carry different costs.

## 1. Respect the interaction contract

- Identify the exact required response format before solving. If the environment requires exactly one JSON action on the final line, provide exactly that action and no competing output format.

- Keep the current instance separate from prior tasks unless the task explicitly says instances recur with the same rule. Repeated task IDs can indicate a learned rule, but do not assume access to prior conversations.
- If the task has a defined terminal action, use it only when the environment says the instance is over or permits ending it.

## 2. Parse the grid before hypothesizing

- Record dimensions, background color, non-background colors, and all repeated shapes.
- Segment objects by 4-neighbor connectivity first. If shapes touch only diagonally, note that 8-neighbor grouping would produce a different interpretation; choose the grouping supported by the examples.
- For repeated blocks, record each object's bounding box and top-left coordinate. Distinguish object origins from individual colored cells, and do not treat overlapping 2x2 windows as separate objects.
- Make a compact inventory: object shape, color, location, size, adjacency, alignments, and any repeated spacing or symmetry.
- For each demonstration, compare input and output cell-by-cell conceptually: determine what changed, what stayed fixed, and whether dimensions or background changed. Treat unchanged examples as constraints too.

## 3. Infer a compact, reusable rule

- Prefer a simple rule that explains every demonstration, not a list of coordinates or a rule fitted only to the latest input.
- Test likely ARC operations: recolor by shape/size/count, select outliers, complete symmetry, connect or group nearby objects, copy/reflect/rotate, sort or move by position, and use one object as a marker or template.
- Check whether selection is at the object, component, row/column, or whole-pattern level. If adjacent identical blocks form a larger connected object, compare both the elementary-block and merged-component interpretations.

- Start from an exact copy of the test grid and apply only the inferred changes.
- Preserve dimensions, row lengths, and every unaffected cell. For recoloring, change all and only the cells belonging to selected objects.

# ARC Puzzle Solving

- Record dimensions, background color, non-background colors, and all repeated shapes.

pos=[(0,0),(0,11),(1,4),(2,7),(5,15),(0,12),(4,3),(4,7),(1,13),(3,8),(4,5),(5,0)]
neg=[(3,1),(3,13),(4,10),(5,6),(1,1),(1,4),(2,9),(0,6),(2,2),(5,11)]

def square(n): return n>=0 and isqrt(n)**2==n
features={
 'r':lambda r,c:r,'c':lambda r,c:c,'r+c':lambda r,c:r+c,'c-r':lambda r,c:c-r,'r*c':lambda r,c:r*c,'c mod r+1':lambda r,c:c%(r+1),

 'r+c+1':lambda r,c:r+c+1,
}
for name,fn in features.items():
 valsP=[fn(*p) for p in pos]; valsN=[fn(*p) for p in neg]

- Prefer a concise object table or coordinate list over repeatedly transcribing whole grids. Mark coordinates clearly as zero- or one-indexed and specify whether they identify top-left cells or component bounds.
- Do not encode an unverified pattern as a rule. A single demonstration may permit many explanations; more data or a safer explicit uncertainty estimate is preferable to false certainty.

## Pitfalls

- Miscounting objects when 2x2 motifs touch or overlap; verify bounding boxes and connectivity.
- Mixing coordinate conventions or describing a component as a singleton when its adjacent blocks make a larger component.
- Inferring selection by location from one sample when the rule may depend on shape, grouping, symmetry, or a relation among objects.
- Spending demo requests without articulating which uncertainty the next example is meant to resolve.
- Submitting prose or extra formatting when the benchmark requires only a machine-readable action.

# ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this workflow for ARC-style grid tasks, including lifelong streams where each instance is independent and demonstrations, wrong submissions, and attempts may carry different costs.

## 1. Respect the interaction contract

- Identify the exact required response format before solving. If the environment requires exactly one JSON action on the final line, provide exactly that action and no competing output format.
- Track demo requests, wrong attempts, and attempt caps. A request for another demonstration is an information-gathering action, not a free pause; use it only when its expected information is worth its cost.
- Keep the current instance separate from prior tasks unless the task explicitly says instances recur with the same rule. Repeated task IDs can indicate a learned rule, but do not assume access to prior conversations.
- If the task has a defined terminal action, use it only when the environment says the instance is over or permits ending it.

## 2. Parse the grid before hypothesizing

- Record dimensions, background color, non-background colors, and all repeated shapes.
- Segment objects by 4-neighbor connectivity first. If shapes touch only diagonally, note that 8-neighbor grouping would produce a different interpretation; choose the grouping supported by the examples.
- For repeated blocks, record each object's bounding box and top-left coordinate. Distinguish object origins from individual colored cells, and do not treat overlapping 2x2 windows as separate objects.
- Make a compact inventory: object shape, color, location, size, adjacency, alignments, and any repeated spacing or symmetry.
- For each demonstration, compare input and output cell-by-cell conceptually: determine what changed, what stayed fixed, and whether dimensions or background changed. Treat unchanged examples as constraints too.

## 3. Infer a compact, reusable rule

- Prefer a simple rule that explains every demonstration, not a list of coordinates or a rule fitted only to the latest input.
- Test likely ARC operations: recolor by shape/size/count, select outliers, complete symmetry, connect or group nearby objects, copy/reflect/rotate, sort or move by position, and use one object as a marker or template.
- Check whether selection is at the object, component, row/column, or whole-pattern level. If adjacent identical blocks form a larger connected object, compare both the elementary-block and merged-component interpretations.
- Explicitly test a candidate against every positive and negative example. Ask: what distinguishes selected objects from visually similar unselected ones? If no stable discriminator is supported, keep uncertainty explicit rather than inventing a confident rule.
- When multiple hypotheses survive, identify what new demonstration would discriminate between them. Request it only if the information gain is likely to prevent a costlier wrong submission.

## 4. Construct and verify the output

- Start from an exact copy of the test grid and apply only the inferred changes.
- Preserve dimensions, row lengths, and every unaffected cell. For recoloring, change all and only the cells belonging to selected objects.
- Before submitting, verify that the output follows the same rule used for all demonstrations, that no object was omitted or accidentally merged, and that the serialized grid contains only integers in the allowed range.
- If feedback says incorrect and the task remains active, use that information to update the hypothesis; do not repeat the same output unchanged.

## 5. Manage reasoning and tool use

- Delegate only genuinely independent analyses, and provide each analyst with the same precise object inventory and exact question. Avoid repeated redundant delegation; compare distinct hypotheses rather than accumulating near-identical guesses.
- Prefer a concise object table or coordinate list over repeatedly transcribing whole grids. Mark coordinates clearly as zero- or one-indexed and specify whether they identify top-left cells or component bounds.
- Do not encode an unverified pattern as a rule. A single demonstration may permit many explanations; more data or a safer explicit uncertainty estimate is preferable to false certainty.

## Pitfalls

- Miscounting objects when 2x2 motifs touch or overlap; verify bounding boxes and connectivity.
- Mixing coordinate conventions or describing a component as a singleton when its adjacent blocks make a larger component.
- Inferring selection by location from one sample when the rule may depend on shape, grouping, symmetry, or a relation among objects.
- Spending demo requests without articulating which uncertainty the next example is meant to resolve.
- Submitting prose or extra formatting when the benchmark requires only a machine-readable action.

## 3. Infer a compact, reusable rule

- Prefer a simple rule that explains every demonstration, not a list of coordinates or a rule fitted only to the latest input.
- Test likely ARC operations: recolor by shape/size/count, select outliers, complete symmetry, connect or group nearby objects, copy/reflect/rotate, sort or move by position, and use one object as a marker or template.
- Check whether selection is at the object, component, row/column, or whole-pattern level. If adjacent identical blocks form a larger connected object, compare both the elementary-block and merged-component interpretations.
- Explicitly test a candidate against every positive and negative example. Ask: what distinguishes selected objects from visually similar unselected ones? If no stable discriminator is supported, keep uncertainty explicit rather than inventing a confident rule.
- When multiple hypotheses survive, identify what new demonstration would discriminate between them. Request it only if the information gain is likely to prevent a costlier wrong submission.

## 4. Construct and verify the output

- Start from an exact copy of the test grid and apply only the inferred changes.
- Preserve dimensions, row lengths, and every unaffected cell. For recoloring, change all and only the cells belonging to selected objects.
- Before submitting, verify that the output follows the same rule used for all demonstrations, that no object was omitted or accidentally merged, and that the serialized grid contains only integers in the allowed range.
- If feedback says incorrect and the task remains active, use that information to update the hypothesis; do not repeat the same output unchanged.

## 5. Manage reasoning and tool use

- Delegate only genuinely independent analyses, and provide each analyst with the same precise object inventory and exact question. Avoid repeated redundant delegation; compare distinct hypotheses rather than accumulating near-identical guesses.
- Prefer a concise object table or coordinate list over repeatedly transcribing whole grids. Mark coordinates clearly as zero- or one-indexed and specify whether they identify top-left cells or component bounds.
- Do not encode an unverified pattern as a rule. A single demonstration may permit many explanations; more data or a safer explicit uncertainty estimate is preferable to false certainty.

## Pitfalls

- Miscounting objects when 2x2 motifs touch or overlap; verify bounding boxes and connectivity.
- Mixing coordinate conventions or describing a component as a singleton when its adjacent blocks make a larger component.
- Inferring selection by location from one sample when the rule may depend on shape, grouping, symmetry, or a relation among objects.
- Spending demo requests without articulating which uncertainty the next example is meant to resolve.
- Submitting prose or extra formatting when the benchmark requires only a machine-readable action.

Use this workflow for ARC-style grid tasks, including lifelong streams where each instance is independent and demonstrations, wrong submissions, and attempts may carry different costs.

## 1. Respect the interaction contract

- Identify the exact required response format before solving. If the environment requires exactly one JSON action on the final line, provide exactly that action and no competing output format.
- Track demo requests, wrong attempts, and attempt caps. A request for another demonstration is an information-gathering action, not a free pause; use it only when its expected information is worth its cost.
- Keep the current instance separate from prior tasks unless the task explicitly says instances recur with the same rule. Repeated task IDs can indicate a learned rule, but do not assume access to prior conversations.
- If the task has a defined terminal action, use it only when the environment says the instance is over or permits ending it.

## 2. Parse the grid before hypothesizing

- Record dimensions, background color, non-background colors, and all repeated shapes.
- Segment objects by 4-neighbor connectivity first. If shapes touch only diagonally, note that 8-neighbor grouping would produce a different interpretation; choose the grouping supported by the examples.
- For repeated blocks, record each object's bounding box and top-left coordinate. Distinguish object origins from individual colored cells, and do not treat overlapping 2x2 windows as separate objects.
- Make a compact inventory: object shape, color, location, size, adjacency, alignments, and any repeated spacing or symmetry.
- For each demonstration, compare input and output cell-by-cell conceptually: determine what changed, what stayed fixed, and whether dimensions or background changed. Treat unchanged examples as constraints too.

## 3. Infer a compact, reusable rule

- Prefer a simple rule that explains every demonstration, not a list of coordinates or a rule fitted only to the latest input.
- Test likely ARC operations: recolor by shape/size/count, select outliers, complete symmetry, connect or group nearby objects, copy/reflect/rotate, sort or move by position, and use one object as a marker or template.
- Check whether selection is at the object, component, row/column, or whole-pattern level. If adjacent identical blocks form a larger connected object, compare both the elementary-block and merged-component interpretations.
- Explicitly test a candidate against every positive and negative example. Ask: what distinguishes selected objects from visually similar unselected ones? If no stable discriminator is supported, keep uncertainty explicit rather than inventing a confident rule.
- When multiple hypotheses survive, identify what new demonstration would discriminate between them. Request it only if the information gain is likely to prevent a costlier wrong submission.

## 4. Construct and verify the output

- Start from an exact copy of the test grid and apply only the inferred changes.
- Preserve dimensions, row lengths, and every unaffected cell. For recoloring, change all and only the cells belonging to selected objects.
- Before submitting, verify that the output follows the same rule used for all demonstrations, that no object was omitted or accidentally merged, and that the serialized grid contains only integers in the allowed range.
- If feedback says incorrect and the task remains active, use that information to update the hypothesis; do not repeat the same output unchanged.

## 5. Manage reasoning and tool use

- Delegate only genuinely independent analyses, and provide each analyst with the same precise object inventory and exact question. Avoid repeated redundant delegation; compare distinct hypotheses rather than accumulating near-identical guesses.
- Prefer a concise object table or coordinate list over repeatedly transcribing whole grids. Mark coordinates clearly as zero- or one-indexed and specify whether they identify top-left cells or component bounds.
- Do not encode an unverified pattern as a rule. A single demonstration may permit many explanations; more data or a safer explicit uncertainty estimate is preferable to false certainty.

## Pitfalls

- Miscounting objects when 2x2 motifs touch or overlap; verify bounding boxes and connectivity.
- Mixing coordinate conventions or describing a component as a singleton when its adjacent blocks make a larger component.
- Inferring selection by location from one sample when the rule may depend on shape, grouping, symmetry, or a relation among objects.
- Spending demo requests without articulating which uncertainty the next example is meant to resolve.
- Submitting prose or extra formatting when the benchmark requires only a machine-readable action.

# ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this workflow for ARC-style grid tasks, including lifelong streams where each instance is independent and demonstrations, wrong submissions, and attempts may carry different costs.

## 1. Respect the interaction contract

- Identify the exact required response format before solving. If the environment requires exactly one JSON action on the final line, provide exactly that action and no competing output format.
- Track demo requests, wrong attempts, and attempt caps. A request for another demonstration is an information-gathering action, not a free pause; use it only when its expected information is worth its cost.
- Keep the current instance separate from prior tasks unless the task explicitly says instances recur with the same rule. Repeated task IDs can indicate a learned rule, but do not assume access to prior conversations.
- If the task has a defined terminal action, use it only when the environment says the instance is over or permits ending it.

## 2. Parse the grid before hypothesizing

- Record dimensions, background color, non-background colors, and all repeated shapes.
- Segment objects by 4-neighbor connectivity first. If shapes touch only diagonally, note that 8-neighbor grouping would produce a different interpretation; choose the grouping supported by the examples.
- For repeated blocks, record each object's bounding box and top-left coordinate. Distinguish object origins from individual colored cells, and do not treat overlapping 2x2 windows as separate objects.
- Make a compact inventory: object shape, color, location, size, adjacency, alignments, and any repeated spacing or symmetry.
- For each demonstration, compare input and output cell-by-cell conceptually: determine what changed, what stayed fixed, and whether dimensions or background changed. Treat unchanged examples as constraints too.

## 3. Infer a compact, reusable rule

- Prefer a simple rule that explains every demonstration, not a list of coordinates or a rule fitted only to the latest input.
- Test likely ARC operations: recolor by shape/size/count, select outliers, complete symmetry, connect or group nearby objects, copy/reflect/rotate, sort or move by position, and use one object as a marker or template.
- Check whether selection is at the object, component, row/column, or whole-pattern level. If adjacent identical blocks form a larger connected object, compare both the elementary-block and merged-component interpretations.
- Explicitly test a candidate against every positive and negative example. Ask: what distinguishes selected objects from visually similar unselected ones? If no stable discriminator is supported, keep uncertainty explicit rather than inventing a confident rule.
- When multiple hypotheses survive, identify what new demonstration would discriminate between them. Request it only if the information gain is likely to prevent a costlier wrong submission.

## 4. Construct and verify the output

- Start from an exact copy of the test grid and apply only the inferred changes.
- Preserve dimensions, row lengths, and every unaffected cell. For recoloring, change all and only the cells belonging to selected objects.
- Before submitting, verify that the output follows the same rule used for all demonstrations, that no object was omitted or accidentally merged, and that the serialized grid contains only integers in the allowed range.
- If feedback says incorrect and the task remains active, use that information to update the hypothesis; do not repeat the same output unchanged.

## 5. Manage reasoning and tool use

- Delegate only genuinely independent analyses, and provide each analyst with the same precise object inventory and exact question. Avoid repeated redundant delegation; compare distinct hypotheses rather than accumulating near-identical guesses.
- Prefer a concise object table or coordinate list over repeatedly transcribing whole grids. Mark coordinates clearly as zero- or one-indexed and specify whether they identify top-left cells or component bounds.
- Do not encode an unverified pattern as a rule. A single demonstration may permit many explanations; more data or a safer explicit uncertainty estimate is preferable to false certainty.

## Pitfalls

- Miscounting objects when 2x2 motifs touch or overlap; verify bounding boxes and connectivity.
- Mixing coordinate conventions or describing a component as a singleton when its adjacent blocks make a larger component.
- Inferring selection by location from one sample when the rule may depend on shape, grouping, symmetry, or a relation among objects.
- Spending demo requests without articulating which uncertainty the next example is meant to resolve.
- Submitting prose or extra formatting when the benchmark requires only a machine-readable action.

## 2. Parse the grid before hypothesizing

- Record dimensions, background color, non-background colors, and all repeated shapes.
- Segment objects by 4-neighbor connectivity first. If shapes touch only diagonally, note that 8-neighbor grouping would produce a different interpretation; choose the grouping supported by the examples.

## 3. Infer a compact, reusable rule

- Prefer a simple rule that explains every demonstration, not a list of coordinates or a rule fitted only to the latest input.

# ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this workflow for ARC-style grid tasks, including lifelong streams where each instance is independent and demonstrations, wrong submissions, and attempts may carry different costs.

## 1. Respect the interaction contract

- Identify the exact required response format before solving. If the environment requires exactly one JSON action on the final line, provide exactly that action and no competing output format.
- Track demo requests, wrong attempts, and attempt caps. A request for another demonstration is an information-gathering action, not a free pause; use it only when its expected information is worth its cost.
- Keep the current instance separate from prior tasks unless the task explicitly says instances recur with the same rule. Repeated task IDs can indicate a learned rule, but do not assume access to prior conversations.
- If the task has a defined terminal action, use it only when the environment says the instance is over or permits ending it.

## 2. Parse the grid before hypothesizing

- Record dimensions, background color, non-background colors, and all repeated shapes.
- Segment objects by 4-neighbor connectivity first. If shapes touch only diagonally, note that 8-neighbor grouping would produce a different interpretation; choose the grouping supported by the examples.

- Prefer a simple rule that explains every demonstration, not a list of coordinates or a rule fitted only to the latest input.

- Start from an exact copy of the test grid and apply only the inferred changes.

## 5. Manage reasoning and tool use

- Delegate only genuinely independent analyses, and provide each analyst with the same precise object inventory and exact question. Avoid repeated redundant delegation; compare distinct hypotheses rather than accumulating near-identical guesses.

# ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this workflow for ARC-style grid tasks, including lifelong streams where each instance is independent and demonstrations, wrong submissions, and attempts may carry different costs.

## 2. Parse the grid before hypothesizing

- Record dimensions, background color, non-background colors, and all repeated shapes.
- Segment objects by 4-neighbor connectivity first. If shapes touch only diagonally, note that 8-neighbor grouping would produce a different interpretation; choose the grouping supported by the examples.
- For repeated blocks, record each object's bounding box and top-left coordinate. Distinguish object origins from individual colored cells, and do not treat overlapping 2x2 windows as separate objects.

- For each demonstration, compare input and output cell-by-cell conceptually: determine what changed, what stayed fixed, and whether dimensions or background changed. Treat unchanged examples as constraints too.

## 3. Infer a compact, reusable rule

- Prefer a simple rule that explains every demonstration, not a list of coordinates or a rule fitted only to the latest input.

# ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this workflow for ARC-style grid tasks, including lifelong streams where each instance is independent and demonstrations, wrong submissions, and attempts may carry different costs.

## 1. Respect the interaction contract

- Identify the exact required response format before solving. If the environment requires exactly one JSON action on the final line, provide exactly that action and no competing output format.
- Track demo requests, wrong attempts, and attempt caps. A request for another demonstration is an information-gathering action, not a free pause; use it only when its expected information is worth its cost.
- Keep the current instance separate from prior tasks unless the task explicitly says instances recur with the same rule. Repeated task IDs can indicate a learned rule, but do not assume access to prior conversations.
- If the task has a defined terminal action, use it only when the environment says the instance is over or permits ending it.

## 2. Parse the grid before hypothesizing

- Record dimensions, background color, non-background colors, and all repeated shapes.
- Segment objects by 4-neighbor connectivity first. If shapes touch only diagonally, note that 8-neighbor grouping would produce a different interpretation; choose the grouping supported by the examples.
- For repeated blocks, record each object's bounding box and top-left coordinate. Distinguish object origins from individual colored cells, and do not treat overlapping 2x2 windows as separate objects.
- Make a compact inventory: object shape, color, location, size, adjacency, alignments, and any repeated spacing or symmetry.
- For each demonstration, compare input and output cell-by-cell conceptually: determine what changed, what stayed fixed, and whether dimensions or background changed. Treat unchanged examples as constraints too.

## 3. Infer a compact, reusable rule

- Prefer a simple rule that explains every demonstration, not a list of coordinates or a rule fitted only to the latest input.
- Test likely ARC operations: recolor by shape/size/count, select outliers, complete symmetry, connect or group nearby objects, copy/reflect/rotate, sort or move by position, and use one object as a marker or template.
- Check whether selection is at the object, component, row/column, or whole-pattern level. If adjacent identical blocks form a larger connected object, compare both the elementary-block and merged-component interpretations.
- Explicitly test a candidate against every positive and negative example. Ask: what distinguishes selected objects from visually similar unselected ones? If no stable discriminator is supported, keep uncertainty explicit rather than inventing a confident rule.
- When multiple hypotheses survive, identify what new demonstration would discriminate between them. Request it only if the information gain is likely to prevent a costlier wrong submission.

## 4. Construct and verify the output

- Start from an exact copy of the test grid and apply only the inferred changes.
- Preserve dimensions, row lengths, and every unaffected cell. For recoloring, change all and only the cells belonging to selected objects.
- Before submitting, verify that the output follows the same rule used for all demonstrations, that no object was omitted or accidentally merged, and that the serialized grid contains only integers in the allowed range.
- If feedback says incorrect and the task remains active, use that information to update the hypothesis; do not repeat the same output unchanged.

## 5. Manage reasoning and tool use

- Delegate only genuinely independent analyses, and provide each analyst with the same precise object inventory and exact question. Avoid repeated redundant delegation; compare distinct hypotheses rather than accumulating near-identical guesses.

- Do not encode an unverified pattern as a rule. A single demonstration may permit many explanations; more data or a safer explicit uncertainty estimate is preferable to false certainty.

## Pitfalls

- Miscounting objects when 2x2 motifs touch or overlap; verify bounding boxes and connectivity.
- Mixing coordinate conventions or describing a component as a singleton when its adjacent blocks make a larger component.
- Inferring selection by location from one sample when the rule may depend on shape, grouping, symmetry, or a relation among objects.
- Spending demo requests without articulating which uncertainty the next example is meant to resolve.
- Submitting prose or extra formatting when the benchmark requires only a machine-readable action.

# ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this workflow for ARC-style grid tasks, including lifelong streams where each instance is independent and demonstrations, wrong submissions, and attempts may carry different costs.

## 1. Respect the interaction contract

- Identify the exact required response format before solving. If the environment requires exactly one JSON action on the final line, provide exactly that action and no competing output format.
- Track demo requests, wrong attempts, and attempt caps. A request for another demonstration is an information-gathering action, not a free pause; use it only when its expected information is worth its cost.
- Keep the current instance separate from prior tasks unless the task explicitly says instances recur with the same rule. Repeated task IDs can indicate a learned rule, but do not assume access to prior conversations.
- If the task has a defined terminal action, use it only when the environment says the instance is over or permits ending it.

## 2. Parse the grid before hypothesizing

- Record dimensions, background color, non-background colors, and all repeated shapes.
- Segment objects by 4-neighbor connectivity first. If shapes touch only diagonally, note that 8-neighbor grouping would produce a different interpretation; choose the grouping supported by the examples.
- For repeated blocks, record each object's bounding box and top-left coordinate. Distinguish object origins from individual colored cells, and do not treat overlapping 2x2 windows as separate objects.
- Make a compact inventory: object shape, color, location, size, adjacency, alignments, and any repeated spacing or symmetry.
- For each demonstration, compare input and output cell-by-cell conceptually: determine what changed, what stayed fixed, and whether dimensions or background changed. Treat unchanged examples as constraints too.

## 3. Infer a compact, reusable rule

- Prefer a simple rule that explains every demonstration, not a list of coordinates or a rule fitted only to the latest input.
- Test likely ARC operations: recolor by shape/size/count, select outliers, complete symmetry, connect or group nearby objects, copy/reflect/rotate, sort or move by position, and use one object as a marker or template.
- Check whether selection is at the object, component, row/column, or whole-pattern level. If adjacent identical blocks form a larger connected object, compare both the elementary-block and merged-component interpretations.
- Explicitly test a candidate against every positive and negative example. Ask: what distinguishes selected objects from visually similar unselected ones? If no stable discriminator is supported, keep uncertainty explicit rather than inventing a confident rule.
- When multiple hypotheses survive, identify what new demonstration would discriminate between them. Request it only if the information gain is likely to prevent a costlier wrong submission.

## 4. Construct and verify the output

- Start from an exact copy of the test grid and apply only the inferred changes.
- Preserve dimensions, row lengths, and every unaffected cell. For recoloring, change all and only the cells belonging to selected objects.
- Before submitting, verify that the output follows the same rule used for all demonstrations, that no object was omitted or accidentally merged, and that the serialized grid contains only integers in the allowed range.
- If feedback says incorrect and the task remains active, use that information to update the hypothesis; do not repeat the same output unchanged.

## 5. Manage reasoning and tool use

- Delegate only genuinely independent analyses, and provide each analyst with the same precise object inventory and exact question. Avoid repeated redundant delegation; compare distinct hypotheses rather than accumulating near-identical guesses.
- Prefer a concise object table or coordinate list over repeatedly transcribing whole grids. Mark coordinates clearly as zero- or one-indexed and specify whether they identify top-left cells or component bounds.
- Do not encode an unverified pattern as a rule. A single demonstration may permit many explanations; more data or a safer explicit uncertainty estimate is preferable to false certainty.

## Pitfalls

- Miscounting objects when 2x2 motifs touch or overlap; verify bounding boxes and connectivity.
- Mixing coordinate conventions or describing a component as a singleton when its adjacent blocks make a larger component.
- Inferring selection by location from one sample when the rule may depend on shape, grouping, symmetry, or a relation among objects.
- Spending demo requests without articulating which uncertainty the next example is meant to resolve.
- Submitting prose or extra formatting when the benchmark requires only a machine-readable action.
